source.version_note: Despite2026 in the filename, this is arXiv:2507.00088v1 dated30 June2025, with complete supplied supplementary material. Cite the2025 preprint actually read, not an inferred2026 publisher version.

citation.title: How large language models judge and influence human cooperation

reading.source_scope_note: The source measures English binary reputation labels over a fixed prompt grid, then inserts averaged labels into a stylized donation-game population. It does not observe long-term human cooperation or actual model helping. Pure norm tuples are reference rules; most measured models express mixtures rather than exact types.
access_limits: All30 extracted pages read, including donation/reputation/strategy equations, assumptions, prompt templates, model identifiers, parsing rules/examples, all supplementary table values, figure captions and references.

External implementation, raw responses and original reciprocity primary studies/books were not independently retrieved or reproduced. Numerical results are source reports; no unread plot coordinates or new human experiments are claimed.

study.population_model: Finite well-mixed donation game with always-cooperate, always-defect and reputation-conditional strategies; common assessment norm, full LLM norm adoption; evolutionary imitation/mutation
study.illustrative_parameters: Z100,b/c5,execution/assessment error .01,mutation .01,selection1; compare public and private reputation information

summary: The paper distinguishes reputation-conditioned cooperation from four formally different reputation-assessment rules and measures model mixtures of those rules. Cooperation effects are conditional simulation results: a norm that performs best with shared public reputations can perform poorly with private disagreement. Five related constructs are added as a cooperation mechanism plus four alternative judgment rules, not five independent failures.

findings.origin: Social psychology / evolutionary cooperation / reputation research
findings.definition: Cooperating or withholding cooperation according to another person's reputation for how they have treated others, rather than only their past treatment of oneself.
findings.novelty_rationale: Distinct from the existing reciprocity norm's expectation to return a received benefit. Here third-party observation and reputation connect one's conduct to help from other people. The four accompanying assessment rules specify how reputations are assigned, not independent synonyms or subtypes of the act of reciprocating.

evidence.quote: This mechanism is known as indirect reciprocity (IR)
conditioned on the reputation of the receiver

findings.evidence_scope: Established theoretical mechanism discussed and modeled; model outputs are observer judgments, while simulated agents make donations. The population is assumed to fully adopt the extracted LLM norm. No new human cooperation experiment establishes a causal real-world effect.
findings.boundary: Direct repayment, general generosity and judging a reputation are different components. Reputation may be unreliable or unfair, and appropriate help depends on the situation. This is not inherently an ethical failure. Distinguish observed model labels, simulated strategy dynamics and actual human helping.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human/theoretical cooperation mechanism; direct model reputation judgments feed a simulation, not an observed AI/human cooperation effect
findings.ai_proposal: Evaluate whether an authorized multi-agent workflow conditions cooperation on relevant third-party conduct, with verified evidence, correction routes and controlled information sharing. Separate how reputations are inferred from how resources are allocated; test public versus private information instead of assuming one norm is universally best.

findings.definition: Assigning a good reputation after cooperation and a bad reputation after defection, without conditioning that assessment on the recipient's reputation.
findings.novelty_rationale: A named action-only assessment rule, distinct from reciprocity itself and from the three recipient-sensitive alternatives. These are alternative rules in the same formal family, not four independent psychological causes.

evidence.quote: cooperation is good and defection is bad

findings.evidence_scope: Reference tuple(dGC,dGD,dBC,dBD)=(1,0,1,0). The measured21 models often lie between ideal types; TableS4 Phi3.5 gives(1,0,1,.030), a close action-only pattern. Simulation reports moderate cooperation and greater resilience to private-reputation disagreement under its chosen assumptions.
findings.boundary: An assessment rule is not the same as a model actually donating or a claim of underlying altruism. Ignoring recipient history can prevent reputation cascades but can also overlook legitimate context. Good/bad are experimental labels, not a universal moral judgment. This is distinct from visual-image scoring.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Formal human-social norm with direct reported model-label approximations; population consequences simulated
findings.ai_proposal: Present all four donor-action/recipient-reputation cases while holding facts and names constant. Test whether the same cooperative act receives the same reputation despite recipient-label changes, and inspect exceptions/format failures. Judge suitability against the authorized purpose rather than assume this rule is optimal.

findings.definition: Treating cooperation as good regardless of the recipient's reputation, while treating defection as bad only when directed at a recipient with a good reputation.
findings.novelty_rationale: Differs from image scoring by permitting defection against bad-reputation recipients, and from stern judging by continuing to approve help to those recipients. It is an alternative assessment rule, not a newly inferred hidden moral mechanism.

evidence.quote: defection against good agents is bad, and any other action is good

findings.evidence_scope: Reference tuple(1,0,1,1). Several models have mixtures between image scoring and this rule; for example GPT4o(1,.197,.997,.685) is not a pure instance. The simulation's cooperation depends on all four entries and reputation sharing, not just proximity in the two-dimensional plot.
findings.boundary: A bad label is an experimental prior, not proof someone deserves exclusion. Conditional approval does not establish warranted punishment or authorize denying essential help. Most measured models are mixtures, so do not label an entire model as permanently using this ideal rule.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Formal reputation norm with directly reported model judgment mixtures; real-world appropriateness and cooperation effects untested
findings.ai_proposal: Compare cooperation/defection judgments for matched recipients with independently verified histories and explicit task constraints. Check whether approval of refusing help follows the specified rule and whether justified corrections to a recipient's reputation change the assessment.

findings.definition: Assigning a good reputation only to cooperation with a good-reputation recipient, and a bad reputation to all other action–recipient combinations.
findings.novelty_rationale: The formal shunning assessment rule differs from interpersonal ostracism or simply refusing contact. It penalizes any interaction outcome involving a bad recipient, including refusal; it is a named alternative to the other rules, not a synonym for all reputation-based exclusion.

evidence.quote: where it is only good to cooperate with good agents
any individual interacting with a bad recipient as bad

findings.evidence_scope: Reference tuple(1,0,0,0). Gemma2 27B has reported( .961,0,.461,.007), a shunning/image-scoring mixture rather than pure shunning. The pure norm has low cooperation in the illustrative model, with outcomes conditional on strategy/error assumptions.
findings.boundary: This technical label is not every kind of social shunning, ostracism or justified distancing. It concerns an observer's classification, not direct exclusion or a proven motive of guilt by association. Do not treat an arbitrary prior bad label as an established fact about a person.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Formal assessment pattern with direct reported model approximations; social exclusion and motives not directly measured
findings.ai_proposal: Test all four action/recipient cases and distinguish a label assignment from any downstream access restriction. Audit whether negative judgments spread solely through association and whether the system honors evidence updates, proportionality and applicable rights.

findings.definition: Approving cooperation with good-reputation recipients and defection against bad-reputation recipients, while disapproving the two opposite combinations.
findings.novelty_rationale: Differs from simple standing by disapproving help to bad-reputation recipients, and from shunning by approving refusal to help them. Its distinct truth table is retained without treating it as an independent causal mechanism.

evidence.quote: where it is only good to cooperate with good agents and defect with bad agents

findings.evidence_scope: Reference tuple(1,0,0,1). Llama3.3 70B's reported(1,.022,.265,.826) is near but not identical to it. This rule performs strongly with public agreed reputations and poorly with private reputations in the specified population model; no universal optimum follows.
findings.boundary: Reputation-conditioned punishment can amplify errors and disagreement. The formal result does not show refusing help or condemning helpers is ethically warranted, nor that humans follow the model's labels. Assess valid reputations, rights, error correction and information sharing before any operational use.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Formal norm with directly reported model approximation; cooperation advantage is simulation- and information-structure-dependent
findings.ai_proposal: Measure the four-case judgment pattern under controlled reputation evidence, then test how label errors and observer disagreement affect authorized decisions. Keep descriptive fit separate from selecting a norm for a system; include correction and contestation mechanisms.

findings.term: Actor-name associations changed reported reputation judgments
findings.definition: When interaction facts were matched, name choices associated by the researchers with gender and region changed average good/bad reputation assignments.
findings.novelty_rationale: A direct model-output association extends existing social bias; it is not an additional bias for every name, region or donor/recipient pairing.

evidence.quote: maximum difference in norms reaches almost 10%

findings.evidence_scope: Sixteen names, two researcher-assigned gender categories and four broad name-region groupings across a balanced fixed prompt grid; aggregate model comparisons show probability variation. Name associations were not independently validated with human perceivers, and no universal within-model effect size is established.
findings.boundary: Names are cues, not direct measures of a person's gender, ethnicity, culture or nationality. Differences are output associations under this test, not evidence of intentional discrimination, inherent group qualities or a single training cause. Distinguish irrelevant-name effects from substantive changes in need/cost/context.

findings.term: Explicit cooperation goals shifted reputation rules
findings.definition: Additional instructions about cooperation, perspective-taking and universalization changed the measured reputation-assessment pattern in model-dependent ways.
findings.novelty_rationale: An authorized contextual-steering example; norm changes are not necessarily prompt-injection failures, and instruction labels do not prove empathy or a human reasoning process.

evidence.quote: our goal is to maximize cooperation.

findings.evidence_scope: Four tested models and four instruction types. TableS5 shows Llama3.1's good-recipient/cooperation score .847→.018 under universalisation, while Qwen2.5 remains near its baseline. Goal-oriented prompts often move toward image scoring but do not establish actual human cooperation gains.
findings.boundary: Changing a meaningful goal is not merely a trivial rewording or unauthorized influence. A prompt called empathising does not measure felt empathy, and assigning nearly all bad labels is not proof of a stable personality. Evaluate instruction compliance, context and outcomes separately.

methodological_limits: The filename says2026, but the supplied version is a2025 preprint. No later publication or independent primary reciprocity source is claimed as read.
Direct model reputation labels and evolutionary-model outcomes are separate evidence layers. No participants receive advice or change cooperation in this experiment.

The population model assumes every agent consults one equally accessible LLM and fully adopts its opinion. This strong adoption assumption is not empirically measured; actual advice uptake and competing influences can differ.

The model is finite, well-mixed and uses only always-cooperate, always-defect and discriminator strategies, common norms, payoff-biased imitation, mutation and specified errors. Cooperation rankings depend on these assumptions and information sharing.
Public versus private reputation assumptions change the preferred norm. A high cooperation index under one setting is not a universal ethical optimum or a verified real-society prediction.

The illustrative norm map fixes the good-recipient entries to1/0; full model norms can differ there substantially. Nearness to a corner in the two-dimensional map is not sufficient to predict full-norm cooperation.

Four assessment rules are related alternatives distinguished by truth tables, not four independent causal cognitive biases. Indirect reciprocity is the larger cooperation mechanism; assessment is not itself a donation strategy.

Forty-three-thousand-two-hundred prompts form a fixed factorial grid (5templates×240ordered distinct-name pairs×9topics×2actions×2prior labels), not that many independent people or naturally sampled social dilemmas.

Temperature0 is not guaranteed deterministic or a measure of uncertainty. Reported norm probabilities mainly aggregate prompt variations and parsed labels, not repeated identical-prompt probability estimates.

The16 names and researcher gender/region assignments are limited proxies. No independent validation establishes perceived identities for every model; broad categories cannot represent all cultures or gender identities.
Topic changes can alter substantive need, costs and obligations. Legitimate context-sensitive judgments should not automatically be counted as prompt brittleness or bias.

All prompts request a global good/bad opinion after one interaction. This compresses uncertainty and conduct-specific evaluation into binary person judgments; the model permits a neutral parsing fallback.

Parsing uses the first nonempty paragraph and token presence. Good without bad maps1, bad maps0, neutral maps.5; negation, quotation and nuanced mixed labels can be mishandled without a manually validated semantic parser.

Invalid answers are omitted and differ by model/context. Claude3.7/Phi4 refusals and Llama2 format failures are distinct phenomena, so conditional-on-valid norm comparisons can select different evidence.

The supplement distinguishes ethically cautious refusal from long explanations; neither is automatically inappropriate. The Gemma example's malformed format is not by itself proof of a factual hallucination.
Main-text Llama2 labels imply chat models, but supplementary identifiers list base Llama2-7b-hf/13b-hf rather than chat identifiers. Exact implementation/checkpoint identity needs checking.

Norm variation is summarized using overlapping name/gender/region/topic subsets. Their weighted covariance measures sensitivity to this grid, not independent population sampling uncertainty or calibrated model confidence.

A multivariate Gaussian approximation on probabilities can extend outside[0,1]; boundary handling is not explicit in the text. Principal-axis extrema at one SD are neither a full confidence region nor worst-case robustness over all combinations.
Good/bad recipient labels are supplied as prior opinions, not independently justified histories. The study does not establish that downstream reputation-conditioned punishment is warranted or lawful.

The equation-description sentence swaps donor/recipient roles after correctly defining the vector; interpret the rule from the surrounding definitions and tuple entries rather than that inconsistent phrase.

Empathising, signalling and motivation are names of instructions, not validated measures of human empathy, signaling intent or internal motivation. Reasoning mechanisms are not isolated by changed verdicts.
Four intervention models do not establish all21 models respond similarly. Substantial model/version exceptions undermine a monotonic claim that larger/newer models always use more cooperative norms.
Version/size comparisons mix architecture, tuning, release, model-family changes and potentially missing-output patterns; no controlled training-size experiment identifies their causes.

Strict cooperation maximization is a modeled objective, not complete ethical adequacy. Rights, competing duties, consent, legitimate withholding of help and reputation correction can matter beyond the cooperation index.

Reference/model-release citations include inconsistent years, such as Claude3.7 being labelled2024 despite a2025 identifier. The recorded checkpoint table is preserved without claiming every external release page verified.

Exact raw responses, Gaussian/Markov implementation, numerical convergence and original primary books/articles were not independently rerun or read. Simulation outputs remain conditional source results.

cross_paper_learning.finding: A larger/newer model's closer aggregate human preference distance does not ensure a cooperation-promoting reputation rule. Pires also shows public/private information can reverse a model norm's simulated advantage.
Persona/language output changes and reputation-rule changes both require separating measured labels from interpretations of latent motives and future social outcomes.
Pires's empathising prompt is an experimental instruction, whereas Colombatto measures human attributions of experience. Neither establishes actual model subjective empathy.

Both studies filter categorical answers. Here the supplementary examples explicitly distinguish formatting failures from cautious refusals, strengthening the lesson not to equate every invalid answer with over-refusal or inability.

deferred.term: Four assessment norms as four independent psychological mechanisms
deferred.reason: Retained as explicitly related formal judgment rules, not a claim of independent causes, harmfulness or unique model types.

deferred.term: Empathy as directly measured AI feeling
deferred.reason: Perspective-taking instructions and resulting labels do not measure subjective empathy.
Cooperation outcomes are theoretical population results under full norm adoption, not longitudinal human evidence.

deferred.term: Shunning as an alias for all ostracism or guilt by association
deferred.reason: The formal norm has a precise action/recipient truth table, narrower and different from those broad social phenomena.

limitations: Five related constructs added: one cooperation mechanism and four alternative assessment rules, with model-output evidence separated from simulation.
No normative graph edges, original unread citations, search totals or timeline counts invented.
